AI’s buzz in trucking is justified: Trimble panel
From left to right: Craig Fuller, FreightWaves; Lee Klaskow, Bloomberg; Alex Formoso, Polyglass; Martin Schmidt, director, sales engineering, at Trimble and moderator of the panel
San Diego–Lee Klaskow, the senior analyst for logistics at Bloomberg, has seen a lot of hyped technology in his years covering the industry.
Many of them have not panned out. But he's sold on AI.
In a morning session on day of the Trimble Insight (NASDAQ: TRMB) conference here, after leading executives at Trimble had spoken of AI much of the morning, Klaskow appeared on a panel with Craig Fuller, the CEO of FreightWaves, and Alex Formoso, the executive vice president for procurement and supply chain at Polyglass U.S.A., which manufacturers roofing products.
"I've been covering this space for some 20-odd years," Klaskow said. "It's the first technology hype that's actually worth the hype."
Remember blockchain?
He rolled through other technologies that have grabbed the spotlight over the years: autonomous vehicles ("we've been talking about autonomous for maybe 25 years") and blockchain. "There's all these other things that came and went," Klaskow said.
"With AI, we're definitely seeing the benefits," Klaskow said. "Whether it's a broker using to let you know there's a missed pickup to figuring out when the next pickup should be, or customer service or rate pricing or route optimization."
He cited the experience of C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW) whose proof of its AI success is evident in its rising revenue and profitability even as it cuts headcount substantially.
Fuller said brokers make the best customers for new technology because "effectively these guys are the day traders of the industry. They're the ones that are most willing to adopt far more than the asset carriers."
Selling any sort of new technology to asset-based carriers, he said, "is a very long sales cycle. They tend to be much more cynical about improvements." But Fuller added that is a natural outcome of being in a business "where you have to pay attention to every penny."
But for brokers, he said, "they're interested in anything that can give them the edge to buy more efficiently."
"There's only two ways to make money in brokerage," Fuller said. "Either your margin expands on a per transaction basis, or you do more loads." But with heightened regulatory scrutiny over what sort of carriers brokers are employing, broker margins are compressing, Fuller said.
"So the only way brokers are going to increase their profits is to do more volume, and AI is a way to help them optimize that solution," he added.
But there was caution on the panel as well. For example, Fuller said he was a board member at a company where AI was implemented with few results to show for it, except for one big negative: the drivers hated it.
"The next board meeting, the management came back and said 'we've gotten no more productivity. In fact we've upset our drivers.'"
The key, he said, is not to put AI "between you and your most important resource."
Formoso said something similar.
Representing the shipper point of view, Formoso said Polyglass is regularly bombarded with emails and phone calls. The format of them is usually the same, as he described it: "You know, we could do everything for you. We are a broker."
The response, Formoso said, is "delete, delete, delete."
But the contrast that does get his attention, Formos said, is a broker that knows, for example, that Polyglass moves product from Texas to Florida "and I see that you do eight or nine per week." A potential backhaul might be offered, he said.
That's a sign the broker has "done a little bit of homework," Formoso said. "Now I'm not just an email."
Fuller, in comments he has made in other forums, said the current freight market is "the most interesting time since deregulation." And one of the reasons, he added, is the opposite of deregulation: "regulatory pressure and oversight, and that's creating a whole new playbook."
Technology and AI are "part of the story," Fuller said, "but I think what's more interesting is how the government is actually interfering in some ways or impacting the freight market in ways that they haven't done in frankly years."

Trucking must rethink workflows as AI expands, Trimble CEO says
Technology supplier introduces new features for routing, fleet management and maintenance software at its 2026 Insight conference
Managing Editor, Features and Multimedia
“The traditional ways of managing freight are changing,” Painter said. (Seth Clevenger/Transport Topics)
Key Takeaways:
Trimble executives said at its Sept. 28 Insight conference in San Diego that companies must redesign workflows and infrastructure to realize AI’s potential.
Trimble said AI can improve efficiency while preserving roles for drivers and experienced transportation professionals, with PC Miler processing 5.5 billion monthly routing requests.
Trimble introduced CoPilot Driver Assistant, Route Orchestration, autonomous planning, Arc Agent skills and upgrades for transportation management, maintenance and yard operations.
[Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.]
SAN DIEGO — Artificial intelligence is beginning to reshape transportation operations, but trucking businesses won’t unlock the full potential of this technology if they simply layer AI tools onto existing workflows, top executives at Trimble told industry technology leaders.
“The traditional ways of managing freight are changing,” CEO Rob Painter said during the Sept. 28 opening session at Trimble’s 2026 Insight conference. “The temptation is to view AI as either an existential threat to our industry or a magic wand that solves everything. I think it’s neither.”
Using a nautical reference, Painter instead likened AI to “modern rigging” that can help transportation companies spot a supply chain storm far in advance instead of reacting to it after running aground.
However, this shift from reactive management to real-time orchestration will require companies to update their business processes and infrastructure.
Painter compared the current AI transformation to another massive technology shift more than a century ago — the adoption of electric power, which displaced the steam engine.
At that time, the steam engine dictated the design of massive factories. The electric motor was cheaper and more efficient, but productivity didn’t truly improve for decades, until a new generation of engineers redesigned the infrastructure around this new power source.
“Today, AI is our electric motor, and the trap that every company faces today is the same: bolting a new power source onto an old operational architecture, using AI to speed up the same tasks and the same legacy processes and wondering why the gains are marginal,” Painter said. “We believe that real productivity requires the grit to redesign how work actually happens.”
Attendees explore the exhibits at Trimble’s 2026 Insight conference. (Seth Clevenger/Transport Topics)
Trimble is undergoing that process internally as it integrates AI across its transportation technology portfolio, he said.
He emphasized that AI implementation is as much about people as technology.
“What is in front of us is as much of a human problem as a technology problem, because technology is fundamentally changing how people work,” Painter said.
He also acknowledged that AI and digital transformation have not reduced the importance of commercial truck drivers, who remain the foundation of the entire industry.
“Freight still moves because a driver got up this morning and did the job,” Painter said.
Michael Kornhauser, vice president of Trimble’s transportation and logistics sector, acknowledged the nervousness that some industry professionals feel toward AI adoption but highlighted the essential role that people and human interaction continue to play in the transportation industry.
“AI is accelerating and multiplying the value we can deliver to our customers … but AI cannot replace the context, the judgment, the decades of experience,” he said. “What AI has is infinite execution power. When we add AI execution into the systems you use every day, you get time back in your day. You find efficiencies that reduce cost. And you get the freedom to focus on your most meaningful work.”
At the conference, Trimble introduced product updates and new capabilities spanning routing, navigation, transportation management systems, maintenance, yard operations and back-office automation.
One prominent announcement was the rollout of CoPilot Driver Assistant, a voice-activated enhancement to Trimble’s CoPilot navigation platform. The company said drivers can use natural-language commands to locate fuel stops and parking options and manage trips within hours-of-service constraints.
For example, a driver who wants to take a rest break can simply ask CoPilot for assistance rather than contact dispatch or navigate through menus. The system then evaluates the route, reviews HOS availability and recommends suitable stopping points.
The company also introduced Route Orchestration for its PC Miler routing platform, which recently marked 40 years since its initial launch. The new capability unifies planning, execution, visibility and settlement functions into a single workflow while helping fleets balance safety, tolls and delivery requirements. Kornhauser said Trimble currently processes 5.5 billion routing requests each month through PC Miler.
Kornhauser introduces the company’s latest product updates. (Seth Clevenger/Transport Topics)
For private fleets, Trimble showcased autonomous planning capabilities within Appian Fleet Assistant. The tool functions as a virtual dispatcher by applying operational rules and automatically generating multistop route plans.
“Your best planners are no longer trapped in repetitive work,” Kornhauser said.
Another focus was Trimble Arc Agent, a general-purpose AI agent the company launched in August. Unlike specialized AI tools on the market, Trimble said Arc Agent is designed as a single conversational interface supported by a growing catalog of transportation-specific skills.
The system can automate core workflows such as order entry, contract intake and a new skill for request-for-quote generation. Users also can build custom skills tailored to their specific operations.
Trimble additionally announced browser-based upgrades to modernize its core carrier transportation management systems — TMW.Suite, TruckMate, Innovative and Fuel Dispatch — and enable more seamless connections with AI agents.
Other updates unveiled at the event included AI-powered invoice scanning enhancements for Trimble’s TMT Fleet Maintenance software and new trailer orchestration capabilities for Trimble Dock & Yard, the company’s dock scheduling and yard management platform.
In summary, Kornhauser said the fundamentals of transportation remain unchanged even as AI expands what trucking and logistics providers can accomplish.
“The heart and soul of transportation has not changed,” he said, “but our ability to transform it has.”

Trimble unveils AI agents and TMS upgrades at Insight 2026
Trimble is betting fleets will adopt AI agents faster if they can keep the legacy software that already runs their operations
Trimble has unveiled nearly 20 new features at its Insight 2026 conference in San Diego, led by AI agents, voice navigation and browser-based versions of its transportation management system (TMS) software. Chief Executive Rob Painter pitched the tools as helping fleets recover time lost to volatile freight markets.
Drivers get CoPilot Driver Assistant, which gives hands-free spoken navigation to fuel stops, parking and hours-of-service limits. Route Orchestration for PC*Miler puts planning, tracking and settlement in one workflow.
Other tools target back-office work. Trimble says its TMT invoice scanner reads 100 vendor invoices per batch, while Arc Agent handles order entry and contract intake for staff approval.
Four legacy TMS platforms, including TMW.Suite and TruckMate, are being rebuilt as cloud-hosted systems that AI agents can work within. Vice President Michael Kornhauser aimed the move at carriers wary of abandoning decades-old software.
“Our mission is to bring innovation directly into customer workflows without forcing disruptive platform overhauls,” said Kornhauser. “Whether modernizing core systems like Trimble® TruckMate® software or delivering route-planning autonomy with Appian, it comes down to a simple value equation — turning human context and AI into value for our customers.”
Arc Agent comes on a single subscription with 10 hours of agent time, with extra hours sold separately. All tools can be previewed at the conference, which ends 29 September 2026.

At Insight 2026, Trimble executives argued that fleets may need to redesign workflows to get more from AI as it introduced new products and enhancements. AI’s value will depend on how fleets combine automation with their people's knowledge.
Deborah Lockridge・Editor and Associate Publisher
Trimble President and CEO Rob Painter talking about artificial intelligence at the opening session of Trimble's Insight conference: “What is in front of us is as much of a human problem as a technology problem, because technology is fundamentally changing how people work.”
Credit:
Trimble executives highlighted the potential necessity for trucking fleets to redesign workflows to maximize the benefits of artificial intelligence.
Insight 2026 served as the platform for Trimble to introduce new AI-driven products and enhancements.
The presentation emphasized the role of AI beyond just accelerating tasks, suggesting a comprehensive integration into fleet operations.
When factories first adopted electric motors, many owners replaced their steam engines with one large motor and kept running the same complex system of belts, shafts, and pulleys. According to Trimble President and CEO Rob Painter, the bigger productivity gains came later, when factories put smaller motors on individual machines and rearranged the work around them.
“Today, AI is our electric motor,” Painter told attendees at the 2026 Trimble Insight Conference in San Diego.
Ad Loading...
His point for trucking fleets: AI can make existing tasks faster. Getting more from it may mean rethinking how work moves between people and systems.
“The trap that every company faces today is the same: bolting a new power source onto an old operational architecture, using AI to speed up the same tasks and the same legacy processes, and wondering why the gains are marginal,” Painter said.
That is a tall order in trucking. A dispatcher’s plan reflects more than the information entered into a transportation management system. It may depend on a customer’s delivery preferences, a driver’s experience with a particular location, or what the team has learned from previous disruptions.
Ad Loading...
Michael Kornhauser, Trimble Transportation & Logistics sector vice president, said that experience remains essential even as AI changes what software can do.
Trimble's Next-Generation TMS Powered by Artificial Intelligence
“AI cannot replace the context, the judgment, the decades of experience,” he said. “What AI has is infinite execution power.”
Kornhauser described the combination as “you plus AI”: People bring the knowledge of how their business works, and AI can put that knowledge to work across more tasks. He said fleets repeatedly tell Trimble they want to spend less time on manual processes, control costs, and have more freedom to pursue growth.
“You bring the experience, and AI brings the speed and scale.”
The phrase “infinite execution power” is an ambitious one. In practice, a fleet still has to decide which rules an AI tool should follow, what information it can use, and when an exception needs a person’s attention.
Ad Loading...
Trimble's Appian Fleet Assistant with autonomous planning acts as a virtual dispatcher.
Credit:
Painter acknowledged the human side of that transition. He asked attendees to show how prepared they felt personally for the AI era, then whether their organizations were as prepared. He called the responses “honest and also pretty humbling.”
“What is in front of us is as much of a human problem as a technology problem,” he said, “because technology is fundamentally changing how people work.”
Kornhauser gave a specific example of the experience that can be hard to capture in software: a veteran private-fleet planner who knows that one customer’s store accepts deliveries only through an alley, before 7 a.m.
If that planner is absent or retires, it may be hard for someone else to put that knowledge into practice.
Trimble’s Appian Fleet Assistant with autonomous planning is designed to use a private or dedicated fleet’s rules about customers, drivers and equipment to build multistop routes.
Ad Loading...
It acts as a virtual dispatcher, capturing operational rules to generate multi-stop route plans in seconds. Planners can review its recommendations or allow it to create plans autonomously, Kornhauser said.
Drivers can use natural language to interact hands-free with the CoPilot Driver Assistant.
Credit:
Trimble also announced Route Orchestration for PC*Miler and CoPilot. It unifies planning, execution, visibility and settlement into a single workflow — balancing safety, tolls and delivery constraints — to optimize outcomes across the entire route lifecycle.
It lets a fleet select and save a preferred route based on factors such as time, distance, tolls, cost, or safety, then send that route to the driver through CoPilot.
Kornhauser’s point was that a route chosen with the operation’s priorities in mind should carry through from planning to execution, rather than remain with one planner or driver.
A new CoPilot Driver Assistant brings a conversational interface into the cab. It provides hands-free, natural-language in-cab navigation to locate fuel and parking and manage HOS limits.
Ad Loading...
Kornhauser gave the example of a tired driver asking the assistant to find a place to stop. Trimble says the assistant considers the route and hours-of-service limits when finding an option.
The company also described ways for drivers to find and reserve parking or lodging through partners.
In the shop, Trimble has expanded TMT AI Invoice Scanning, which reads vendor PDF invoices and enters information into the maintenance system.
Reduce time spent inputting invoices in TMT's maintenance software.
Credit:
It can now process batches of up to 100 invoices and help map parts and repairs to VMRS codes, Kornhauser said. That could reduce the time spent entering repair paperwork, although fleets would still need to check how well it handles their vendors’ invoices.
Trimble Dock & Yard addresses a different handoff: what happens as a truck approaches and moves through a facility.
Ad Loading...
Its Advanced Trailer Orchestration connects appointments, updated arrival times, and trailer moves so carrier, transportation, and warehouse teams can work from the same information. It's designed to eliminate blind spots between the road and the facility and create a single shared record for every trailer — from gate to dock
Kornhauser described the aim as “a shared version of what’s actually happening when the truck reaches the yard.”
Advanced Trailer Orchestration connects appointments, updated arrival times, and trailer moves
Credit:
Trimble is also updating its TMW.Suite, TruckMate, Innovative and Fuel Dispatchtransportation management systems. Trimble said the cloud-hosted architectures preserve decades of operational logic while providing cleaner, browser-accessible interfaces that enable collaboration between people and AI agents.
The changes include browser-based workflows, more ways to connect with other software, and a way for AI agents to access permitted tools and information within the TMS.
Tips for Successful AI Adoption for Trucking Companies
Kornhauser said the products are at different points in that work. He showed examples ranging from a modernized customer service workflow in TruckMate to billing screens in TMW.Suite and dispatch workflows in Fuel Dispatch.
Ad Loading...
The keynote also highlighted Trimble TMS, its native cloud solution built for growing North American full-truckload carriers and small and medium-sized enterprises.
Trimble’s pitch to existing customers is that they can gain new capabilities while keeping the configurations and processes built into their systems over the years.
Why VMRS Is the Natural Link Between AI, Predictive Analytics, and Vehicle Repairs [Commentary]
Trimble Arc Agent, launched in August, is designed to work across such processes.
The company describes it as an "AI digital colleague" that automates repetitive, multi-step operational tasks through one conversational interface. Arc Agent automates core workflows — such as Order Entry, Contract Intake, and the new Intelligent RFQ Builder skill.
Its built-in skills include preparing orders for entry into a TMS, pulling terms from rate contracts for review, and organizing shipment data for a request for quotes. Fleets can also use its custom skill-building feature to digitize and automate complex processes like payroll reconciliation.
Ad Loading...
Trimble says Arc Agent operates within permissions and business rules set by the customer. Its actions are recorded, and exceptions go back to a person. Those controls matter if an agent is going to do more than suggest the next step.
The announcements give fleets a range of tasks to examine, from an invoice that needs entering to a route that needs rebuilding.
Painter’s electric motor analogy asks a larger question of each one: Will AI simply help someone complete the existing process faster, or prompt the fleet to change the process?

Trimble Navigation, a supplier of a family of GPS products to the maritime and other industries, has been the recipient of many contracts of late. In April, Trimble signed a $1.3 million contract with the U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) to provide GPS Integrity Monitoring Stations for use in the USCG's Differential Global Positioning System (DGPS). The USCG's DGPS system is designed to provide navigation information for coastal areas, harbors and waterways of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and most of Alaska and Hawaii free of charge. Trimble's 4000IM MSK Integrity Monitors will verify that the system is broadcasting correct and accurate navigation messages to recreational boaters, commercial shipping and fishing fleets, workboats, and cruise ships. In addition, surveyors and mappers, environmental consultants, police, and emergency response vehicles with ready GPS equipment will be capable of receiving the USCG's broadcast signal.
More recently, Trimble was awarded a contract with the USCG to provide 326 NT200CG GPS receivers for use in the USCG's Aids to Navigation (ATON) vessels. Differential GPS positioning information from Trimble's NT200CG will be used to place and maintain more than 50,000 buoys, day markers and lights throughout the U.S. coastal waters. Trimble's NT200CG — a custom unit based on Trimble's NT200D — allows USCG vessels to quickly and precisely position these navigational aides.
Other Business Aside from its contracts with the USCG, Trimble has negotiated several other cooperative agreements within the past year.
In March, the company announced its $24 million deal with American Mobile Satellite Corp. (AMSC), a contract which called for Trimble to supply its Galaxy/GPS land mobile satellite communications terminals for use in AMSC's Mobile Messaging Service Network. Delivery of the contract started in May, and will continue into 1996.
At the end of 1994 Trimble signed on with the Finnish Board of Navigation (FBoN) to provide reference station and integrity monitors for the radio beacon- based DGPS marine navigation systems of Finland and Estonia. The FBoN planned to install Trimble's 4000MSK DGPS Reference Station and 4000 IM MSK Integrity Monitors along the coasts of Finland and Estonia. At the time, this announcement brought to 14 the number of countries that had chosen Trimble's DGPS Reference Stations and Integrity Monitors for accurate positioning and coastal navigation.

Trimble keeps freight business sale on the table while unveiling new AI tools
Trimble's strategic review of its transportation and logistics business is ongoing, with multiple parties still interested, even as the company rolls out new freight technology for fleet customers. Pictured is Trimble CEO Rob Painter delivering the opening keynote Monday at the company's Insight 2026 conference in San Diego. (Photo: FreightWaves)
SAN DIEGO — Trimble's review of its transportation and logistics business remains underway, and multiple outside parties remain interested in the unit, CEO Rob Painter said Monday at the company's Insight 2026 conference.
Painter offered no timetable or indication that a sale has become more likely. Asked whether the review could also include a spinoff, he said its purpose was to determine what would be best for customers, employees and shareholders.
"There is no update," Painter told reporters at an executive media round table. "Most strategic reviews end up with continuing to do what we do." He said Trimble is operating the business as usual and that he is "super, super … comfortable to be the ongoing owner of the business."
Trimble (Nasdaq: TRMB) disclosed in August that it had received credible, unsolicited interest from multiple parties and had launched a strategic review with financial adviser Goldman Sachs. Painter confirmed Monday that the review is ongoing and, when asked whether interest still exists from multiple parties, answered: "Yes to everything you said."
Painter characterized the transportation unit as a scarce asset with a distinctive network and technology portfolio, saying Trimble has an obligation as a public company to consider credible approaches.
"It's not surprising to me that we've had inbound interest," Painter said. "It's a scarce asset, a scarce set of capabilities. We're a public company. We have a fiduciary obligation to the shareholders to listen if we have credible interest."
Trimble has not indicated when the review will conclude or what its ultimate outcome might be.
"We hope to wrap up the review," he said. "I'm super comfortable if I'm back in front of you again in weeks, months, or a year from now at our next conference and we're executing the playbook because that's how we're operating right now."
Painter also left open the possibility that the strategic review could result in the transportation business becoming a separate company.
He declined to speculate about what Trimble's exposure to trucking would look like if the transportation business were ultimately sold.
"My view is this is a Trimble business and let's say until it's not, if that's the case," Painter said. "I'm super, super — I can't emphasize that enough — comfortable to be the ongoing owner of the business."
"This business is a terrific business with an exciting future providing real value and unique value," he added.
Trimble pushes AI into existing trucking systems
The comments came as Trimble used its annual Insight conference to demonstrate that investment in the transportation segment is continuing during the strategic review.
The company unveiled technologies centered on voice AI, route and trailer orchestration, automated maintenance and transportation management systems designed to support AI agents.
Michael Kornhauser, who leads Trimble's transportation operations in North America and its applications business, said the company's modernization strategy is intended to let existing customers begin using AI without undergoing expensive, disruptive replacements of longstanding TMS platforms.
Trimble's latest TMS release provides an updated experience designed to support AI while allowing fleets to retain existing systems and integrations.
"We felt that that was the quickest way to get our customers in their existing systems to a place where AI can impact their business today," Kornhauser said.
The approach means customers don't have to immediately disconnect technology and integrations accumulated over decades, he said.
"For now, there's not a big lift. There's not a big risk," Kornhauser said.
Trimble executives also highlighted Arc Agent, which the company is developing around a single AI agent capable of acquiring multiple skills rather than deploying separate agents for individual tasks.
Philipp Pfister, vice president of Transporeon- a Trimble company, described Arc Agent as functioning somewhat like another employee: Users can teach it a task, verify its work and gradually give it greater responsibility as trust develops.
The goal is for Arc Agent to operate across freight processes ranging from procurement and execution to settlement and across shippers, carriers, brokers and other participants.
Trimble said customers will also be able to create skills tailored to their own operations instead of relying exclusively on predefined applications.
Kornhauser cited one example involving currency conversion for TMT Trucking. A capability that he said traditionally might have required a three- to six-month proof of concept, custom coding and professional services was created in Arc in roughly 35 minutes.
"You don't have to have an engineering degree to build a skill," Pfister said.
Painter acknowledged that adoption of autonomous AI also introduces questions about governance, cybersecurity and protection of proprietary information.
Customers can connect Trimble and non-Trimble data, he said, but businesses experimenting with AI quickly encounter questions about controlling access and preventing sensitive data from escaping their organizations.
"Pretty quickly, you go from, wow, this is pretty cool to wait a minute, how are we going to govern this?" Painter said.
He said Trimble spends "tens and tens of millions of dollars every year" on cyber resilience.
Pfister said Arc Agent incorporates a human-in-the-loop model in which users can approve actions and provide feedback, while the system maintains a trail of actions that can be reviewed.
"The data of our customers is like the number one priority that we have," Pfister said. "We need to protect the data of our customers at any point in time."
Trimble is also expanding technology aimed at increasingly complex U.S.-Mexico freight movements.
Asked during the roundtable how AI and orchestration technology could improve cross-border freight, Kornhauser pointed first to Trimble's mapping and routing capabilities.
"We're doing a lot to enhance our Mexico Maps data," he said.
Trimble has roughly 6 million mapped places in North America and is adding more locations in Mexico, particularly truck-relevant points associated with cross-border movements.
Kornhauser said improved mapping can give carriers greater visibility into cross-border shipments, while Trimble's TMS products also support those movements.
"We see the same thing — there's an increased volume, there's a lot of complexity," Kornhauser said.
The Mexico investments underscore the scope of the transportation technology operation Trimble is considering whether to retain, spin off or potentially sell.
Painter, however, emphasized that no decision has been made.
For now, Trimble executives said they are continuing to invest in the business, including integrating capabilities from Transporeon, which Trimble acquired in 2023.
Painter described that acquisition as a strategic success and said its capabilities give Trimble a platform to connect different participants and processes across freight transportation.
"We think it's got a bright future ahead of it," Painter said.
Why it matters: Multiple parties remain interested in Trimble's freight technology business, but its CEO says the strategic review has no announced outcome, as the company continues to roll out new AI-powered freight technology.

Why Is Trimble (TRMB) Down 1.2% Since Last Earnings Report?
It has been about a month since the last earnings report for Trimble Navigation (TRMB). Shares have lost about 1.2% in that time frame, outperforming the S&P 500.
Will the recent negative trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is Trimble due for a breakout? Well, first let's take a quick look at its most recent earnings report in order to get a better handle on the recent drivers for Trimble Inc. before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late.
Trimble Q2 Earnings Beat Estimates on Field Systems Strength
Trimble reported second-quarter 2026 non-GAAP earnings of 86 cents per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 7.5%. Earnings rose 21.1% year over year.
Revenues of $972 million increased 11% year over year and up 10% on an organic basis.
The company also surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 2.2%. The quarter benefited from organic execution in AECO and Field Systems. Annualized recurring revenue (ARR) reached a record $2.51 billion, up 14% year over year and 12% organically.
TRMB's Revenue Mix Keeps Recurring Streams in Focus
Subscription and services revenues were $640.6 million, up 9.9% year over year, while product revenues advanced 13.2% to $331.4 million. Subscription and services accounted for 65.9% of total revenues, keeping recurring streams central to the business mix.
Management said recurring revenue growth supported stronger gross and operating profitability. The Connect & Scale strategy remains focused on linking data and workflows across Trimble's software and hardware ecosystem.
Trimble's AECO Growth Draws on Cross-Sell and AI
AECO revenues were $388.5 million, with organic growth of 9%. Segment ARR reached a record $1.57 billion and increased 14% organically. Trimble Construction One bundles, cross-sell activity, and the Document Crunch acquisition supported bookings momentum.
The segment's operating income margin was 30.6%, up 20 basis points year over year.
Management said AECO remains on track for an operating margin of about 35% in 2026, while new AI tools are being deployed across estimating, job costing, and contract-risk workflows.
TRMB's Field Systems Leads Segment Momentum
Field Systems generated $442.5 million in revenue, with 12% organic growth. ARR was $399 million, also up 12% organically. Demand was strongest in Civil Construction and Geospatial, led by data centers, utilities, and energy infrastructure.
Tariff refunds reduced revenues by $14 million, creating a three-percentage-point drag on growth, but had no impact on operating income. The segment's operating margin expanded 210 basis points to 32.9%, helped by recurring revenue growth and scale.
Trimble's T&L Unit Posts Growth Amid Freight Pressure
Transportation & Logistics revenues were $141 million, up 5% organically, while ARR increased 7% to $533 million. Transporeon delivered mid-teens growth, and management cited healthy bookings despite a still-constrained freight market.
Operating margin improved 240 basis points to 24%. Trimble also began a strategic review of the T&L business after receiving inbound interest from multiple parties, with management emphasizing that there is no predetermined outcome or timeline.
TRMB's Profitability Expands With Revenue Growth
Non-GAAP gross margin increased 120 basis points year over year to 71.8%.
Adjusted EBITDA reached $278 million, with margin expanding 120 basis points to 28.6%. GAAP results included a $562 million goodwill impairment related to T&L, which drove a GAAP net loss of $471.7 million.
Non-GAAP operating income was $260.6 million, translating to a 26.8% margin, up 140 basis points.
Trimble's Cash Flow Supports Capital Returns
TRMB ended the quarter with $214.4 million in cash and equivalents and total debt of $1.459 billion.
Through the first two quarters of 2026, operating cash flow was $515 million. Free cash flow totaled $501.8 million for the first half.
The board authorized a new $1 billion share repurchase program, replacing the prior authorization, while share repurchases totaled $329 million through the first two quarters.
TRMB Raises 2026 Outlook and Sets Q3 View
Trimble raised its 2026 revenue outlook in the range of $3.90-$3.95 billion and non-GAAP earnings of $3.60-$3.70 per share. Organic ARR growth is expected to be between 12% and 14%, with non-GAAP operating margin projected to be 28.2%-28.6% and adjusted EBITDA margin to be 29.7%-30.1%.
For the third quarter, TRMB expects revenues of $953-$978 million and non-GAAP earnings of 83-88 cents per share. Organic ARR growth is projected to be in the range of 11%-13%. Field Systems ARR growth is expected to face a 400-500 basis-point headwind for several quarters from replacing a low-margin white-label product with an internally developed solution.
How Have Estimates Been Moving Since Then?
In the past month, investors have witnessed a downward trend in estimates review.
Currently, Trimble has a nice Growth Score of B, a grade with the same score on the momentum front. However, the stock has a score of D on the value side, putting it in the bottom 40% for value investors.
Overall, the stock has an aggregate VGM Score of B. If you aren't focused on one strategy, this score is the one you should be interested in.
Estimates have been broadly trending downward for the stock, and the magnitude of these revisions indicates a downward shift. Notably, Trimble has a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). We expect an above average return from the stock in the next few months.

San Diego–Lee Klaskow, the senior analyst for logistics at Bloomberg, has seen a lot of hyped technology in his years covering the industry.
Many of them have not panned out. But he's sold on AI.
In a morning session on day of the Trimble Insight (NASDAQ: TRMB) conference here, after leading executives at Trimble had spoken of AI much of the morning, Klaskow appeared on a panel with Craig Fuller, the CEO of FreightWaves, and Alex Formoso, the executive vice president for procurement and supply chain at Polyglass U.S.A., which manufacturers roofing products.
"I've been covering this space for some 20-odd years," Klaskow said. "It's the first technology hype that's actually worth the hype."
Remember blockchain?
He rolled through other technologies that have grabbed the spotlight over the years: autonomous vehicles ("we've been talking about autonomous for maybe 25 years") and blockchain. "There's all these other things that came and went," Klaskow said.
"With AI, we're definitely seeing the benefits," Klaskow said. "Whether it's a broker using to let you know there's a missed pickup to figuring out when the next pickup should be, or customer service or rate pricing or route optimization."
He cited the experience of C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW) whose proof of its AI success is evident in its rising revenue and profitability even as it cuts headcount substantially.
Fuller said brokers make the best customers for new technology because "effectively these guys are the day traders of the industry. They're the ones that are most willing to adopt far more than the asset carriers."
Selling any sort of new technology to asset-based carriers, he said, "is a very long sales cycle. They tend to be much more cynical about improvements." But Fuller added that is a natural outcome of being in a business "where you have to pay attention to every penny."
But for brokers, he said, "they're interested in anything that can give them the edge to buy more efficiently."
"There's only two ways to make money in brokerage," Fuller said. "Either your margin expands on a per transaction basis, or you do more loads." But with heightened regulatory scrutiny over what sort of carriers brokers are employing, broker margins are compressing, Fuller said.
"So the only way brokers are going to increase their profits is to do more volume, and AI is a way to help them optimize that solution," he added.
But there was caution on the panel as well. For example, Fuller said he was a board member at a company where AI was implemented with few results to show for it, except for one big negative: the drivers hated it.
"The next board meeting, the management came back and said 'we've gotten no more productivity. In fact we've upset our drivers.'"
The key, he said, is not to put AI "between you and your most important resource."
Formoso said something similar.
Representing the shipper point of view, Formoso said Polyglass is regularly bombarded with emails and phone calls. The format of them is usually the same, as he described it: "You know, we could do everything for you. We are a broker."
The response, Formoso said, is "delete, delete, delete."
But the contrast that does get his attention, Formos said, is a broker that knows, for example, that Polyglass moves product from Texas to Florida "and I see that you do eight or nine per week." A potential backhaul might be offered, he said.
That's a sign the broker has "done a little bit of homework," Formoso said. "Now I'm not just an email."
Fuller, in comments he has made in other forums, said the current freight market is "the most interesting time since deregulation." And one of the reasons, he added, is the opposite of deregulation: "regulatory pressure and oversight, and that's creating a whole new playbook."
Technology and AI are "part of the story," Fuller said, "but I think what's more interesting is how the government is actually interfering in some ways or impacting the freight market in ways that they haven't done in frankly years."

Trucking must rethink workflows as AI expands, Trimble CEO says
Technology supplier introduces new features for routing, fleet management and maintenance software at its 2026 Insight conference
Managing Editor, Features and Multimedia
“The traditional ways of managing freight are changing,” Painter said. (Seth Clevenger/Transport Topics)
Key Takeaways:
Trimble executives said at its Sept. 28 Insight conference in San Diego that companies must redesign workflows and infrastructure to realize AI’s potential.
Trimble said AI can improve efficiency while preserving roles for drivers and experienced transportation professionals, with PC Miler processing 5.5 billion monthly routing requests.
Trimble introduced CoPilot Driver Assistant, Route Orchestration, autonomous planning, Arc Agent skills and upgrades for transportation management, maintenance and yard operations.
[Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.]
SAN DIEGO — Artificial intelligence is beginning to reshape transportation operations, but trucking businesses won’t unlock the full potential of this technology if they simply layer AI tools onto existing workflows, top executives at Trimble told industry technology leaders.
“The traditional ways of managing freight are changing,” CEO Rob Painter said during the Sept. 28 opening session at Trimble’s 2026 Insight conference. “The temptation is to view AI as either an existential threat to our industry or a magic wand that solves everything. I think it’s neither.”
Using a nautical reference, Painter instead likened AI to “modern rigging” that can help transportation companies spot a supply chain storm far in advance instead of reacting to it after running aground.
However, this shift from reactive management to real-time orchestration will require companies to update their business processes and infrastructure.
Painter compared the current AI transformation to another massive technology shift more than a century ago — the adoption of electric power, which displaced the steam engine.
At that time, the steam engine dictated the design of massive factories. The electric motor was cheaper and more efficient, but productivity didn’t truly improve for decades, until a new generation of engineers redesigned the infrastructure around this new power source.
“Today, AI is our electric motor, and the trap that every company faces today is the same: bolting a new power source onto an old operational architecture, using AI to speed up the same tasks and the same legacy processes and wondering why the gains are marginal,” Painter said. “We believe that real productivity requires the grit to redesign how work actually happens.”
Attendees explore the exhibits at Trimble’s 2026 Insight conference. (Seth Clevenger/Transport Topics)
Trimble is undergoing that process internally as it integrates AI across its transportation technology portfolio, he said.
He emphasized that AI implementation is as much about people as technology.
“What is in front of us is as much of a human problem as a technology problem, because technology is fundamentally changing how people work,” Painter said.
He also acknowledged that AI and digital transformation have not reduced the importance of commercial truck drivers, who remain the foundation of the entire industry.
“Freight still moves because a driver got up this morning and did the job,” Painter said.
Michael Kornhauser, vice president of Trimble’s transportation and logistics sector, acknowledged the nervousness that some industry professionals feel toward AI adoption but highlighted the essential role that people and human interaction continue to play in the transportation industry.
“AI is accelerating and multiplying the value we can deliver to our customers … but AI cannot replace the context, the judgment, the decades of experience,” he said. “What AI has is infinite execution power. When we add AI execution into the systems you use every day, you get time back in your day. You find efficiencies that reduce cost. And you get the freedom to focus on your most meaningful work.”
At the conference, Trimble introduced product updates and new capabilities spanning routing, navigation, transportation management systems, maintenance, yard operations and back-office automation.
One prominent announcement was the rollout of CoPilot Driver Assistant, a voice-activated enhancement to Trimble’s CoPilot navigation platform. The company said drivers can use natural-language commands to locate fuel stops and parking options and manage trips within hours-of-service constraints.
For example, a driver who wants to take a rest break can simply ask CoPilot for assistance rather than contact dispatch or navigate through menus. The system then evaluates the route, reviews HOS availability and recommends suitable stopping points.
The company also introduced Route Orchestration for its PC Miler routing platform, which recently marked 40 years since its initial launch. The new capability unifies planning, execution, visibility and settlement functions into a single workflow while helping fleets balance safety, tolls and delivery requirements. Kornhauser said Trimble currently processes 5.5 billion routing requests each month through PC Miler.
Kornhauser introduces the company’s latest product updates. (Seth Clevenger/Transport Topics)
For private fleets, Trimble showcased autonomous planning capabilities within Appian Fleet Assistant. The tool functions as a virtual dispatcher by applying operational rules and automatically generating multistop route plans.
“Your best planners are no longer trapped in repetitive work,” Kornhauser said.
Another focus was Trimble Arc Agent, a general-purpose AI agent the company launched in August. Unlike specialized AI tools on the market, Trimble said Arc Agent is designed as a single conversational interface supported by a growing catalog of transportation-specific skills.
The system can automate core workflows such as order entry, contract intake and a new skill for request-for-quote generation. Users also can build custom skills tailored to their specific operations.
Trimble additionally announced browser-based upgrades to modernize its core carrier transportation management systems — TMW.Suite, TruckMate, Innovative and Fuel Dispatch — and enable more seamless connections with AI agents.
Other updates unveiled at the event included AI-powered invoice scanning enhancements for Trimble’s TMT Fleet Maintenance software and new trailer orchestration capabilities for Trimble Dock & Yard, the company’s dock scheduling and yard management platform.
In summary, Kornhauser said the fundamentals of transportation remain unchanged even as AI expands what trucking and logistics providers can accomplish.
“The heart and soul of transportation has not changed,” he said, “but our ability to transform it has.”

Trimble keeps freight business sale on the table while unveiling new AI tools
Trimble's strategic review of its transportation and logistics business is ongoing, with multiple parties still interested, even as the company rolls out new freight technology for fleet customers. Pictured is Trimble CEO Rob Painter delivering the opening keynote Monday at the company's Insight 2026 conference in San Diego. (Photo: FreightWaves)
SAN DIEGO — Trimble's review of its transportation and logistics business remains underway, and multiple outside parties remain interested in the unit, CEO Rob Painter said Monday at the company's Insight 2026 conference.
Painter offered no timetable or indication that a sale has become more likely. Asked whether the review could also include a spinoff, he said its purpose was to determine what would be best for customers, employees and shareholders.
"There is no update," Painter told reporters at an executive media round table. "Most strategic reviews end up with continuing to do what we do." He said Trimble is operating the business as usual and that he is "super, super … comfortable to be the ongoing owner of the business."
Trimble (Nasdaq: TRMB) disclosed in August that it had received credible, unsolicited interest from multiple parties and had launched a strategic review with financial adviser Goldman Sachs. Painter confirmed Monday that the review is ongoing and, when asked whether interest still exists from multiple parties, answered: "Yes to everything you said."
Painter characterized the transportation unit as a scarce asset with a distinctive network and technology portfolio, saying Trimble has an obligation as a public company to consider credible approaches.
"It's not surprising to me that we've had inbound interest," Painter said. "It's a scarce asset, a scarce set of capabilities. We're a public company. We have a fiduciary obligation to the shareholders to listen if we have credible interest."
Trimble has not indicated when the review will conclude or what its ultimate outcome might be.
"We hope to wrap up the review," he said. "I'm super comfortable if I'm back in front of you again in weeks, months, or a year from now at our next conference and we're executing the playbook because that's how we're operating right now."
Painter also left open the possibility that the strategic review could result in the transportation business becoming a separate company.
He declined to speculate about what Trimble's exposure to trucking would look like if the transportation business were ultimately sold.
"My view is this is a Trimble business and let's say until it's not, if that's the case," Painter said. "I'm super, super — I can't emphasize that enough — comfortable to be the ongoing owner of the business."
"This business is a terrific business with an exciting future providing real value and unique value," he added.
Trimble pushes AI into existing trucking systems
The comments came as Trimble used its annual Insight conference to demonstrate that investment in the transportation segment is continuing during the strategic review.
The company unveiled technologies centered on voice AI, route and trailer orchestration, automated maintenance and transportation management systems designed to support AI agents.
Michael Kornhauser, who leads Trimble's transportation operations in North America and its applications business, said the company's modernization strategy is intended to let existing customers begin using AI without undergoing expensive, disruptive replacements of longstanding TMS platforms.
Trimble's latest TMS release provides an updated experience designed to support AI while allowing fleets to retain existing systems and integrations.
"We felt that that was the quickest way to get our customers in their existing systems to a place where AI can impact their business today," Kornhauser said.
The approach means customers don't have to immediately disconnect technology and integrations accumulated over decades, he said.
"For now, there's not a big lift. There's not a big risk," Kornhauser said.
Trimble executives also highlighted Arc Agent, which the company is developing around a single AI agent capable of acquiring multiple skills rather than deploying separate agents for individual tasks.
Philipp Pfister, vice president of Transporeon- a Trimble company, described Arc Agent as functioning somewhat like another employee: Users can teach it a task, verify its work and gradually give it greater responsibility as trust develops.
The goal is for Arc Agent to operate across freight processes ranging from procurement and execution to settlement and across shippers, carriers, brokers and other participants.
Trimble said customers will also be able to create skills tailored to their own operations instead of relying exclusively on predefined applications.
Kornhauser cited one example involving currency conversion for TMT Trucking. A capability that he said traditionally might have required a three- to six-month proof of concept, custom coding and professional services was created in Arc in roughly 35 minutes.
"You don't have to have an engineering degree to build a skill," Pfister said.
Painter acknowledged that adoption of autonomous AI also introduces questions about governance, cybersecurity and protection of proprietary information.
Customers can connect Trimble and non-Trimble data, he said, but businesses experimenting with AI quickly encounter questions about controlling access and preventing sensitive data from escaping their organizations.
"Pretty quickly, you go from, wow, this is pretty cool to wait a minute, how are we going to govern this?" Painter said.
He said Trimble spends "tens and tens of millions of dollars every year" on cyber resilience.
Pfister said Arc Agent incorporates a human-in-the-loop model in which users can approve actions and provide feedback, while the system maintains a trail of actions that can be reviewed.
"The data of our customers is like the number one priority that we have," Pfister said. "We need to protect the data of our customers at any point in time."
Trimble is also expanding technology aimed at increasingly complex U.S.-Mexico freight movements.
Asked during the roundtable how AI and orchestration technology could improve cross-border freight, Kornhauser pointed first to Trimble's mapping and routing capabilities.
"We're doing a lot to enhance our Mexico Maps data," he said.
